A native of the district, Zhang had lived at home since his dismissal. Having recently learned that the Court had approved the reinstatement of former officials, he had been seeking influence and connections everywhere. Chancing upon Yucun, he therefore hastened to congratulate him. After exchanging courtesies, Zhang Rugui told Yucun the news. Yucun was naturally delighted; after a hurried exchange of a few words, they took leave and each returned home. When Leng Zixing heard this, he promptly offered a plan: Yucun should ask Lin Ruhai to appeal on his behalf to Jia Zheng in the capital. Yucun understood his meaning, took his leave, and returned to his lodgings, where he at once found a court gazette and confirmed that the report was true.

p.src: The next day, he discussed the matter with Ruhai in person. Ruhai said, “Providence has arranged things most conveniently. Since my wife passed away, my mother-in-law in the capital has been concerned that my young daughter has no one to depend upon or oversee her upbringing. She previously sent servants of both sexes and boats to fetch her, but my daughter had not yet fully recovered, so she could not depart. I was just thinking that I had not yet repaid the kindness you have shown in teaching her. Now that this opportunity has arisen, how could I fail to do my utmost to repay you? Please set your mind at ease. I have already made the necessary arrangements and written a letter of recommendation, entrusting the matter to my brothers-in-law and asking them to give you every assistance. Only thus can I offer some small token of my sincerity. I have also clearly explained in my letter to them whatever customary expenses may be required, so you need not trouble yourself over that either.” Yucun repeatedly bowed and thanked him profusely, then asked, “May I inquire what offices your distinguished relatives presently hold? I fear that, being inexperienced and careless, I ought not rush into the capital and presume upon them.” Ruhai smiled. “As for my wife’s family, they belong to the same clan register as you. They are grandsons of Duke Rong. My elder brother-in-law, Jia She, courtesy name Enhou, has inherited the title of General of the First Rank. My second brother-in-law, Jia Zheng, courtesy name Cunzhou, is currently an assistant director in the Ministry of Works. He is modest, courteous, and generous, with much of his grandfather’s character. He is no frivolous, pampered official from a wealthy family, which is why I am willing to write and entrust your affair to him. Otherwise, not only might your spotless integrity be sullied, but I myself would disdain to act so.” Only after hearing this did Yucun believe what Zixing had told him the previous day, and he thanked Lin Ruhai once more. Ruhai then said, “I have chosen the second day of next month for my daughter’s journey to the capital. If you travel with her, would that not be convenient for you both?” Yucun assented obediently, inwardly delighted beyond measure. Ruhai then prepared gifts and arranged a farewell feast, all of which Yucun accepted.

p.src: As for his pupil Daiyu, she had only just recovered and could not bear to leave her father. But her maternal grandmother insisted that she come, and Ruhai also told her, “Your father is nearly fifty and has no intention of taking another wife. You are often ill and still very young, with no mother above you to instruct and nurture you, and no sisters or brothers beside you to support you. If you now go and depend upon your grandmother, uncles, and cousins, you will relieve me of much anxiety. Why, then, do you say you will not go?” Only after hearing this did Daiyu take tearful leave of him. p.src: In due course they reached the capital and entered the imperial city. Yucun first straightened his robes and cap, then took a young attendant and, carrying a calling card that identified him as a clansman’s nephew, presented himself at the gate of the Rong Mansion. By then Jia Zheng had read his brother-in-law’s letter and immediately invited Yucun in to meet him. He found Yucun imposing in appearance and refined in speech. Jia Zheng had always cherished scholars, treated the worthy with courtesy and humility, and aided the weak and distressed, in this strongly resembling his grandfather. Moreover, Yucun came commended by his brother-in-law, so Jia Zheng treated him with exceptional favor and exerted all his influence at Court on his behalf. When the memorial was submitted, he easily secured for Yucun reinstatement pending a vacancy. Within two months the prefectural post at Yingtian in Jinling fell vacant, and he obtained that appointment for him. Yucun took leave of Jia Zheng and, choosing an auspicious day, departed to assume office. But that is another matter.

p.src: To return to Daiyu: when she left the boat and stepped ashore that day, sedan chairs and carts for the luggage, sent by the Rongguo Mansion, had long been waiting. Lin Daiyu had often heard her mother say that her maternal grandmother’s household was unlike other families. Even the few third-rank serving women she had seen recently were extraordinary in their food, clothing, and daily provisions; what, then, must the household itself be like? She therefore watched every step and remained constantly on her guard, unwilling to utter one unnecessary word or take one needless step, lest anyone laugh at her. Once seated in the chair, she entered the city and peered out through its gauze window. The bustling streets and dense population were indeed unlike those anywhere else. After travelling for quite some time, she suddenly saw two great stone lions crouching on the north side of the street. Behind them stood a three-bay gate crowned with beast-head ornaments, before which sat a dozen or so men in splendid caps and gorgeous robes. The main gate was closed, and people entered and left only through the side gates at its eastern and western corners. Above the main gate hung a tablet bearing five large characters: “Ningguo Mansion, Built by Imperial Command.” Daiyu thought, “This must be the residence of Grandfather’s elder branch.” As she reflected, they continued westward. Not far away stood another similar three-bay gate; this was the Rongguo Mansion. They did not enter through the main gate, but went in by the western side gate. The bearers carried the chair inside for about the distance of an arrow shot. Just as they were about to turn a corner, they set it down and withdrew. The elderly women following behind had already left their chairs and now hurried forward. Three or four neatly dressed young pages of seventeen or eighteen replaced the bearers and lifted the chair once more. The elderly women walked around the chair and accompanied it to a festooned inner gate, where it was set down. The young pages withdrew. The elderly women came forward, raised the chair curtain, and helped Daiyu alight. Holding an elderly woman’s hand, Lin Daiyu passed through the festooned gate. Covered galleries curved along both sides; in the center stood an entrance hall, where a large marble screen in a red sandalwood frame had been placed. Beyond the screen was a small three-bay hall, and behind it lay the great courtyard of the main inner apartments. Facing them stood five principal rooms, all with carved beams and painted rafters. Side rooms and covered galleries extended through the wings on either side, where parrots, thrushes, and other birds of many kinds hung in cages. Several maidservants dressed in red and green sat upon the raised stone terrace. As soon as they saw the party arrive, they all hurried forward with smiling faces and said, “The Old Lady was asking about you only a moment ago, and here you are at just the right time.” Three or four of them vied to raise the door curtain, while from within came the announcement, “Miss Lin has arrived.”

Just as she was about to bow, her grandmother gathered her into her arms and, crying, “My heart! My precious flesh and blood!” burst into loud sobs. Grandmother Jia then said, “Send for the young ladies. A guest has arrived from afar today, so they need not attend their lessons.” The attendants acknowledged the order, and two of them went off.

p.src: Before long, three nursemaids and five or six maids arrived, surrounding and escorting three young ladies. The first was slightly plump and of medium height; her cheeks had the fresh bloom of lychees and her nose the smooth softness of goose fat. Gentle and reserved, she inspired affection at first sight. The second had sloping shoulders, a slender waist, and a tall, graceful figure. Her face was oval, her eyes bright and her brows finely drawn; every glance sparkled with life, and her refined brilliance made one forget the vulgar world. The third was not yet fully grown and still looked very young. All three wore the same ornaments, skirts, and jackets. Daiyu hurriedly rose to greet them. After they had exchanged courtesies and learned who each other was, everyone resumed their seats. The maids poured tea. Their conversation concerned how Daiyu’s mother had fallen ill, how physicians had been summoned and medicines administered, and how her death and funeral had been attended to. Inevitably, Grandmother Jia was overcome with grief once more. “Of all my children,” she said, “your mother was the one I loved most. Now she has left me before her time, and I could not even see her face once more. How can the sight of you fail to break my heart?” As she spoke, she drew Daiyu into her arms and began sobbing again. Everyone hastened to comfort and console her, and at last her grief subsided a little.

p.src: Though Daiyu was young in years and appearance, everyone saw that there was nothing commonplace in her speech or bearing. Frail as her body and face appeared, she possessed a natural air of grace and refinement, and they realized that she suffered from some constitutional weakness. They therefore asked, “What medicine do you usually take? Why has the illness not been treated without delay?” Daiyu replied, “I have always been like this. I began taking medicine as soon as I could eat and have never stopped to this day. Any number of famous physicians have been invited to revise prescriptions and prepare medicines, but none has had any effect. When I was three, I heard that a scabby-headed monk came and offered to take me away to become a nun, but of course my parents refused. Then he said, ‘If you cannot bear to part with her, I fear her illness will never be cured throughout her life. If she is to recover, from this day onward she must never be allowed to hear the sound of weeping; and apart from her parents, she must never see any relative or friend bearing another surname. Only then may she pass her life in peace.’ He was raving mad and spoke such absurd nonsense that no one paid him any heed. I still take Ginseng Nourishing Vitality Pills now.” Grandmother Jia said, “That is fortunate. We are having pills prepared here at this very moment. We need only tell them to prepare an extra batch.”

p.src: Before she had finished her tea, a maid in a red silk jacket and a blue satin, piped waistcoat came in and said with a smile, “Madam asks Miss Lin to come and sit with her.” Hearing this, the old nurse led Daiyu out again and took her to the three small main rooms along the eastern gallery. Lady Wang, however, was seated at the lower place on the western side, likewise upon a somewhat worn blue satin backrest and cushion. When she saw Daiyu enter, she invited her to take the place on the east. Daiyu guessed at once that this must be Jia Zheng’s seat. Seeing three chairs in a row beside the kang, each draped with a somewhat worn patterned cover, Daiyu sat down on one of them. Only after Lady Wang repeatedly took her by the hand and urged her onto the kang did she sit beside her aunt. Lady Wang said, “Your uncle has gone to observe a fast today, so you may meet him another time. But there is one thing above all that worries me: I have a bane and scourge of a son, the ‘Demon King of Chaos’ of this household. He has gone to a temple today to fulfil a vow and has not yet returned; when you see him this evening, you will understand. From now on, simply pay him no attention; even these cousins of yours dare not provoke him.”

p.src: Daiyu had often heard her mother speak of a cousin born to her second aunt with a piece of jade in his mouth, who was exceptionally unruly, loathed studying, and delighted above all in idling among the women’s apartments; her grandmother doted on him so excessively that no one dared discipline him. Hearing Lady Wang speak in this way, she knew that this was the cousin she meant. She therefore replied with a smile, “Aunt, do you mean the cousin who was born with the jade in his mouth? At home I often heard Mother say that he is a year older than I am and that his childhood name is Baoyu. Although he is exceedingly foolish and mischievous, she said he is very good to his sisters. Besides, now that I am here, I shall naturally live only with my female cousins, while the young gentlemen will have separate courtyards and rooms. How could I possibly become entangled with him?” Lady Wang smiled. “You do not understand. He is unlike other boys. Ever since childhood, because the old lady doted on him, he has been pampered and brought up together with his sisters. If the girls ignore him for a day, he is actually quieter. Even if he feels slighted, he merely goes beyond the inner gate, takes his temper out in private on his two little pages, and grumbles for a while until it passes. But if on some day the girls say even one extra word to him, his heart leaps for joy and he stirs up no end of trouble. That is why I am warning you not to pay him any attention. One moment he pours out sweet words, the next he speaks with no regard for heaven or anyone else, and then he acts like a lunatic or a fool. Whatever he says, do not believe him.”

p.src: Daiyu promised to heed everything she had said. Just then a maid came in to announce, “The old lady’s household says that supper is served.” Lady Wang promptly took Daiyu by the hand and led her westward through the rear door and along the back gallery. Beyond a corner gate lay a broad passage running north and south. To the south stood a small three-bay projecting hall facing the opposite way; to the north rose a large white-painted screen wall, behind which were a half-sized gate and a modest set of rooms. Lady Wang pointed it out to Daiyu with a smile. “That is your Cousin Feng’s apartment. In future, you may come here to find her. If you lack anything, you need only tell her.” At the gate to this courtyard stood four or five young pages, scarcely old enough to have their hair tied in knots, waiting respectfully with hands lowered. Lady Wang then led Daiyu through an east-west passage hall, beyond which lay Grandmother Jia’s rear courtyard. They entered by the rear door, where many attendants were already waiting. Only when they saw Lady Wang arrive did they begin setting out the tables and chairs. Jia Zhu’s widow, Lady Li, served the rice, Xifeng laid out the chopsticks, and Lady Wang presented the soup. Grandmother Jia sat alone on the couch facing the room, with four empty chairs, two on either side. Xifeng hastily drew Daiyu to the first chair on the left, but Daiyu repeatedly declined the honor. Grandmother Jia laughed. “Your aunts and your sisters-in-law do not dine here. You are our guest, so that is precisely where you should sit.” Only then did Daiyu ask permission and take her seat. Grandmother Jia told Lady Wang to be seated. Only after Yingchun and her two sisters had asked permission to sit did they come forward. Yingchun took the first chair on the right, Tanchun the second on the left, and Xichun the second on the right. Maids stood nearby holding a fly whisk, a rinsing bowl, and towels. Lady Li and Xifeng stood beside the table, serving the dishes and urging everyone to eat. Although many married servants and maids waited in the outer room, not so much as a cough could be heard. The meal ended in silence, and maids brought tea to each of them on small trays. Lin Ruhai had taught his daughter that, to cherish her blessings and preserve her health, she must wait until every grain of rice had been swallowed and allow some time to pass before drinking tea, lest she harm her spleen and stomach. But Daiyu had already observed that many customs here differed from those in her own home. Since she had no choice but to conform, she knew she must gradually alter her habits, and so she accepted the tea. She soon saw someone bring a rinsing bowl, so she followed the others and rinsed her mouth. When they had washed their hands, tea was brought again; this time it was tea to drink. Grandmother Jia then said, “You may all go now and leave us to talk at our ease.” At this, Lady Wang rose at once, exchanged a few more casual remarks, and then left with Xifeng and Lady Li. Grandmother Jia then asked Daiyu what books she was studying. Daiyu replied, “I have only just begun the Four Books.” Daiyu in turn asked what books her cousins were reading. Grandmother Jia replied, “What books could they be reading? They merely know a few characters, enough not to be blind with their eyes open!”

On his head he wore a purple-gold crown set with jewels over his bound hair, and across his brow a golden band depicting two dragons contesting a pearl. His bright-red, close-sleeved riding coat was patterned with butterflies flitting among flowers in two shades of gold; at his waist was a multicolored silken palace cord adorned with floral knots and long tassels. Over it he wore a dark-blue figured satin jacket embroidered with eight roundels and edged with tassels, and on his feet were small court boots of blue satin with white soles. His face was as radiant as the mid-autumn moon, his complexion as fresh as flowers at a spring dawn. His temples seemed cut with a knife, his brows painted in ink, his cheeks were like peach petals, and his eyes like autumn waters. Even in anger he seemed to smile, and even his fiercest glare held tenderness. Around his neck hung a gold chi-dragon necklace, together with a five-colored silken cord from which a beautiful piece of jade was suspended. At the sight of him Daiyu was greatly startled and thought, “How very strange! It is as though I have seen him somewhere before. Why does he look so extraordinarily familiar?” Baoyu paid his respects to Grandmother Jia, who told him, “Go and see your mother.” Baoyu turned and went at once. When he returned a little later, he had changed out of his ceremonial dress. All his natural charm gathered at the tips of his brows, and a lifetime’s wealth of feeling dwelt in the corners of his eyes.
His outward appearance was exceedingly fine, yet his true nature was hard to fathom.
Later generations composed two lyrics to the tune “Moon over the West River” that judged Baoyu most aptly. They read:

p.src: Grandmother Jia laughed. “You changed out of your clothes before even meeting our guest. Go and greet your cousin at once!” Baoyu had already noticed the new girl and guessed that she must be his Aunt Lin’s daughter, so he hastened forward and bowed. After they had exchanged greetings and resumed their seats, he studied her closely and found her unlike all the others: two gently curved brows, seeming to frown yet not to frown, hung like wisps of smoke; her pair of dewy eyes seemed to weep yet not to weep. Sorrow dwelt in her dimples, and frailty pervaded her delicate form. Tears glimmered in her eyes, and her delicate breath came faintly. In repose she was like a lovely flower reflected in water; in motion, like a slender willow yielding to the wind. Her mind had one more aperture than the subtle heart of Bigan, and her frailty surpassed even that of the beauty Xizi by three degrees. When Baoyu had finished looking at her, he smiled and said, “I have met this cousin before.” Grandmother Jia laughed. “There you go talking nonsense again! When could you possibly have met her?” Baoyu smiled. “Though I have never actually met her, her face seems so familiar that in my heart I already count her as an old acquaintance. We may as well regard today as a reunion after a long separation.” Grandmother Jia laughed. “So much the better! If that is how you feel, you will be all the more affectionate toward each other.” Baoyu went and sat beside Daiyu, looked her over carefully once more, and asked, “Cousin, have you studied?” “No,” said Daiyu. “I attended school for only a year and can recognize just a few characters.” Baoyu asked, “Which two characters make up your honored name?” Daiyu told him her name. Baoyu then asked for her courtesy name. “I have none,” Daiyu replied. Baoyu smiled. “I shall give you an excellent courtesy name. Nothing could be finer than the two characters ‘Pinpin,’ meaning ‘Knitted Brows.’” Tanchun asked him where that came from. Baoyu replied, “The Comprehensive Study of People Past and Present says: ‘In the west there is a stone called dai, which may be used in place of ink for painting the brows.’ Besides, Cousin Lin’s brows are delicately knitted. Would it not be doubly apt to choose these two characters?” Tanchun laughed. “I fear that is another of your inventions.” Baoyu laughed. “Apart from the Four Books, so much has been invented. Why must I alone be accused of invention?” Then he asked Daiyu, “Do you have a jade too?” No one understood what he meant. Daiyu, however, reasoned that because he had a jade, he was asking whether she had one too, and replied, “I do not have such a thing. I suppose that jade is a rare object. How could everyone possess one?” On hearing this, Baoyu was instantly seized by one of his fits of madness. He tore off the jade and hurled it violently away, cursing, “What rare object? It cannot even distinguish worthy people from unworthy ones, and yet they call it ‘Numinous’! Numinous indeed! I do not want this wretched thing either!” Everyone was terrified and rushed forward together, scrambling to pick up the jade. In alarm, Grandmother Jia gathered Baoyu into her arms and cried, “You wicked creature! If you are angry, it is easy enough to strike or scold someone. Why throw away the very root of your life?”

p.src: His face streaming with tears, Baoyu sobbed, “None of the sisters and cousins at home has one; I alone do, and that is no fun. Now even this fairy-like cousin who has come to us does not have one. That proves it is no good thing.” Grandmother Jia hastened to soothe him. “Your cousin did have one originally. When your aunt died, she could not bear to part from your cousin, and there was no other remedy, so she took her jade away with her. In the first place, this fulfilled the rites of burial and allowed your cousin to show her filial devotion; in the second, your aunt’s spirit could regard it for the time being as though she were seeing her daughter. That is why she only says she has none—she does not wish to boast of it herself. How can you compare yourself with her now? Put it back on carefully at once, or beware when your mother hears of this.” As she spoke, she took the jade from the maid’s hand and fastened it on him herself. Hearing this, Baoyu thought it over and found it entirely reasonable, so he raised no further objection.

p.src: Presently, the nurse came to ask where Daiyu was to be lodged. Grandmother Jia said, “For now, Baoyu shall move out and stay with me in the warm inner chamber, while your young mistress Lin is temporarily settled in the Blue-Gauze Cabinet. Once the last of winter is past, we shall prepare rooms for them in the spring and arrange matters afresh.” Baoyu said, “Dear Grandmother, I shall be perfectly comfortable on the bed outside the Blue-Gauze Cabinet. Why should I move out and disturb your peace?” Grandmother Jia considered this for a moment and said, “Very well, then.” Each was attended by one nurse and one maid, while the others kept watch in the outer room, ready to answer a call. Meanwhile, Xifeng had already ordered a lotus-root-pink flowered bed-curtain and several brocade quilts, satin mattresses, and the like to be sent over.

p.src: Daiyu had brought only two attendants with her: Nanny Wang, who had nursed her since infancy, and a ten-year-old maid named Xueyan, who had likewise been at her side since childhood. Grandmother Jia saw that Xueyan was very young and thoroughly childish, while Nanny Wang was extremely old; judging that neither could attend to Daiyu entirely to her satisfaction or spare her much trouble, she gave Daiyu one of her own second-rank maids, named Yingge. In other respects, Daiyu was provided for on the same scale as Yingchun and the others: besides the nurse who had cared for her from infancy, each young lady had four matrons to instruct and guide her; besides two personal maids responsible for jewelry, washing, and bathing, each also had five or six junior maids to sweep the rooms and run errands. Thus Nanny Wang and Yingge attended Daiyu inside the Blue-Gauze Cabinet. Baoyu’s nurse, Nanny Li, and his senior maid, Xiren, attended him on the large bed outside.

p.src: Xiren, it turned out, had also been a maid of Grandmother Jia, and her original name was Zhenzhu. Because Grandmother Jia doted on Baoyu, she feared that none of his maids would serve him with wholehearted loyalty. She had always liked Xiren for her honest, kindly nature and conscientious devotion to her duties, so she gave her to Baoyu. When Baoyu learned that her family name was Hua, and recalled the line from an old poem, “The fragrance of flowers assails the senses,” he sought Grandmother Jia’s permission and renamed her Xiren. Xiren had a certain single-mindedness about her: while serving Grandmother Jia, she had eyes and heart for Grandmother Jia alone; now that she served Baoyu, she had eyes and heart for Baoyu alone. But because Baoyu was so eccentric and contrary, she was forever remonstrating with him and was deeply troubled at heart.

p.src: That night, after Baoyu and Nanny Li had gone to sleep, Xiren saw that Daiyu and Yingge were still awake inside. Having removed her own ornaments, she slipped quietly in and asked with a smile, “Why have you not gone to sleep yet, miss?” Daiyu promptly invited her in: “Please sit down, sister.” Xiren sat down on the edge of the bed. Yingge said with a smile, “Miss Lin was grieving here just now, weeping and wiping her tears as she said, ‘I arrived only today, yet I have already brought on one of your young master’s mad fits. If he had broken that jade, would it not have been my fault?’ That was why she was so distressed. I had a hard time comforting her.” Xiren said, “Please do not take it so to heart, miss. I fear you will see even stranger and more ridiculous things than this in days to come! If every time he behaves like this you brood over it and grieve, there will be no end to your grieving. Do stop worrying!” Daiyu said, “I shall remember what you have told me. But what, after all, is the origin of that jade? And are there really characters inscribed upon it?” Xiren replied, “No one in the whole family knows where it came from. It even has a hole ready-made in it, and I have heard that when he was born, it was taken from his mouth. Wait until I bring it for you to see; then you will understand.” Daiyu hastily stopped her: “Never mind. It is late now; tomorrow will be soon enough to see it.” They talked a while longer before finally retiring for the night.

p.src: The next morning, after paying her respects to Grandmother Jia, Daiyu went to Lady Wang’s quarters. She found Lady Wang and Xifeng together, opening and reading letters from Jinling; two married female servants sent by Lady Wang’s elder brother and sister-in-law had also come to speak with them. Although Daiyu did not know the circumstances, Tanchun and the others all understood that they were discussing Xue Pan—the son of their maternal aunt of the Xue family in Jinling, and thus their cousin—who, relying on his wealth and power, had beaten a man to death and was now under investigation by the Yingtian prefectural court. Their maternal uncle Wang Ziteng had now received word of the affair and had therefore sent members of his household to inform this side of the family, intending to summon them to the capital.
